en: Your mother fell headfirst.
Since Manas went to the other world,
Ajybai and Khan Bakai were absent.
When Chyiyrdy tried to walk,
Her strength was gone; she had no power.
There was no forest to flee into,
There were no Nogai to turn to for support.
When her son Manas was alive,
The elder woman's greatness was beyond compare.
When she was battered and suffering,
To provide her a nest,
There were no Argyn or Kyrgyz here.
There was no sheltered bank to lie beneath,
No food to put in the orphan's mouth.
Seen today, gone tomorrow—
This deceitful world, so scant in faithfulness,
So this is what the shitty world is like!
With no tongue left to speak,
She grew dazed and lost consciousness.
The elder woman fainted
And fell limply to the ground.
Let us leave her thus;
Now let us begin on the other side.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey,
Left alone with herself,
Parted from her slayer of foes,
At thirty-two years of age.
Kanykey left in mourning,
Semetey left an orphan.
“As though I could let my guard fall—
Is my precious hero here?
Let me devise a firm plan.
That child of Kara Kung, the dark slavewoman,
Let me ask for him, saying, ‘I shall lay him in the cradle.’
Like the morning star at dawn,
Let me make him a guiding sign.
My little one left by the generous hero,
For Semetey, all alone,
Let me give him a companion.
It is God's decree;
Now let me see what is written upon my brow!
For the pennant fastened to a spear,
The hoof left behind by the noble steed,
For the little one, the splendid warhorse,
If he travels on a distant journey,
Let me make him a swift steed.
For my precious Semetey,
Let me make your child a brother.
If you honor the plane tree,
Kara Kung, give me your child, let me see him.
Semetey's painted cradle—
Let me lay him in the painted cradle.
Until the Seven Wild Sheep stars set,
Let me nurse your child seven times in turn
And rear your child to full strength.
When he enters battle, no bullet can pierce
The white armored coat I shall lay upon him.
Semetey and this child
Were both born on the same day.
Let me rear them as twins.
When the two were born,
When my slayer of foes held their feast,
Russians ate at their feast and departed,
Saying, ‘If these two live safely,
They will overthrow the Oirats.’
When he held the feast for the two,
Chinese ate at their feast and departed,
Saying, ‘If the two grow up together,
They will overthrow the world.’
When my precious gray-maned hero was alive,
He made no distinction between the boys,
Calling them little ones gained at the brink of death.
‘If I die, these children—’
Let me not leave an orphan in the wilderness,
The lamp left by Manas, the falcon.
For the gift left by the generous hero,
For the hoof left by the noble steed,
Calling him the hoof to remain behind,
He had horses driven from the hills,
Had a pale-gray mare brought,
Slaughtered a thousand black mares with white blazes,
Young horses and camel yearlings nearing their prime,
And camels from among the camel herds.
Mottled yellow like starlings,
He caught and slaughtered yearlings from the horse herds.
One was named Semetey,
The other was named Zhoobuzar.
He gave them their names together,
Saying, ‘They will be support after me.’
My gray-maned hero dispelled all his sorrow.”
Hearing these words, Kara Kung—
The devil take her!—was seized by a devil.
To the lady whom none would insult,
She hurled an insult.
“Woman, I will not hear your words.
My Kobosh will gouge out your eyes;
Abyke will destroy your camp.
Bitch, he will wipe out all trace of you.
As a wife, you overturned custom and ruined the people;
As a girl, you shook the world and ruined the land.
You have never given up your wildness;
Of the hero Manas, the gray-maned wolf,
You could never have enough wealth.
As though I were indifferent to my child!
You need Semetey dearly;
Do I have no need of my child at all?!
Raging slave, I will not agree to what you say;
I will not give you my child.”
Saying these words then,
Like a black ram lamb,
Kara Kung strutted;
Like a male black crow,
Kara Kung strutted stiffly then.
When she heard Kara Kung's words,
Your dear sister-in-law was shamed.
Raiding the Argyn and throwing them into turmoil,
At Kara Kung's hands,
She thought, “Now let me die.”
Her ribs came apart;
Her heart was terribly troubled:
“My leopard prince, if only you had not died!
Oh God, you let the goose be eaten by a bird of prey.
My own slavewoman Kara Kung,
You made her call me a shameless shrew.
That dear bird called the swan,
You let it be eaten by a harrier.
My companion, my prince, if only you had not died!
My peers, companions and sisters-in-law,
You made them call me a ruined woman.
Damn your father's grave, Kara Kung!
Let me cut off your head;
Let me offer you as a sacrifice!”
Before Kara Kung could flee,
Kanykey seized her then.
At the slanting lower ribs,
At this side of the lung,
For six calves and four yearlings
She had bought Ak-Tinte;
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Drove it home then.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Killed Kara Kung then.
At the edge of the hearth,
Bending her double at the waist,
She buried her out of sight then.
Kara Kung's Zhoobuzar—
She rested his head against a golden forehead ornament,
Wrapped his feet in pure gold coins.
She nursed him at her right breast;
Your sister-in-law stood without hesitation.
As she nursed the child,
To scatter all the wealth,
Your sister-in-law lengthened her stride,
Carrying Zhoobuzar,
To flee toward Zhoon-Dobo,
Nursing the children as her own offspring,
To wander away to Khan Temir,
Your sister-in-law formed her plan:
Before the destroyers entered,
To get away to Kara Khan.
Before your sister-in-law could flee the palace,
Pale-mottled pennants, red banners,
A clamor of “Boi, boi!”
Crescent standards, red banners,
A tumult of battle cries.
All the hills rang with shouting;
When she listened closely,
They were crying the battle cry “Kobosh!”
All the ridges rang with shouting;
When your sister-in-law turned and looked,
They were crying the battle cry “Kochkor!”
May God never show us such a sight!
The spearheads clashed,
And human heads were struck off.
They swayed along the bank,
They surged over the ground,
A flood denser than reeds,
Many hundreds of people.
Those forty companions left by Manas,
Forty dog-companions from forty different places—
Had not one come from Altai,
Had not one come from Khangai,
Had not one come from China,
Had not one come from Crimea?
Calling a hawk to the lure,
The forty companions paid no heed to the spirit.
Drawing bows, they sent a rain of arrows;
The forty companions fired shots like hail.
Roaring in fury,
Effacing the name of Khan Manas,
All cried the battle cry “Kobosh!”
The great host came pouring on.
Baichoro, riding Telkyzyl,
Saw the accursed ones.
Girding his broad battle belt about his waist,
He went alone into the attack.
The reason he went alone:
He was God's beloved servant.
Manas and Baichoro
Were sons of two brothers.
He turned Telkyzyl's head;
Honoring Manas's spirit,
He had been watching over the palace.
That the scoundrels Abyke and Kobosh
Had become enemies, he did not know.
“A deep pit has been dug,” he thought;
Night had fallen upon his head.
“It must be a host from Beijing,” he thought.
Roaring in fury,
Then crying the battle cry “Manas!”
Driving the great host back,
He attacked again and scattered them.
To Chyibyt and Kochkor
He came faster than an arrow;
On reaching them, the two
He struck in succession as he passed.
When Baichoro cried “Manas!”
All the villains,
Shouting, “Kobosh, Kobosh, Kobosh!”
Raised the battle cry “Kobosh!”
Those forty companions left by Manas,
Drawing bows, sent a rain of arrows.
Upon Baichoro then,
They all came pouring.
Chyibyt and Kochkor, two scoundrels,
Adybai and Kolbai, making four—
All of them arrived.
When the great host came pouring on,
When light struck the earth,
When dawn broke clear,
Telkyzyl beneath him
Stumbled as he went.
Those forty companions left by Manas,
Striking with battle axes and clubs,
Reached Baichoro then.
Baichoro, who honored the spirit,
Fell into their hands.
Baichoro then said:
“Forty wolves who were companions,
Do not dig my pit.
Do not make it boil, elder brothers,
My misery from far away.
Do not bring turmoil upon my head,
Such a spectacle as no one would make.
Do not spill my blood;
Forty uncles, do not take away my strength.
Do not cut short my living soul;
Do not let my blood flow like water.
My forty lion-uncles,
I have known your might.
Of Manas, gone to the other world,
I have preserved the ways.
For one day I stood against you;
For Manas, whose spirit is golden,
I fought only for his spirit.
He who gave horses to the horseless,
